blocks.text: A class should have one reason to change: it answers to a single actor, not to everything it happens to do.

Martin's later wording is about **actors**, the people or teams whose requirements drive change. If finance, HR and operations can each force an edit to the same class, those edits collide. **Cohesion** is measured by what changes together, not by how few methods a class has.

items: **Reason to change:** a stakeholder's rule, not a code feature.
**Smell:** a class imported by unrelated teams, or constant merge conflicts in one file.
**Fix:** separate by axis of change, then compose the pieces.

blocks.text: "Does one thing" is a misreading. A class with ten methods that all change for the same reason is cohesive and fine.

walkthrough.note: `InvoiceBefore` changes for three audiences: pricing rules, presentation and persistence. Edits for one can break the others.
The domain object keeps only what changes with business rules: lines and totals. It is immutable, so it is safe to share.
Presentation moves out. A new layout or locale is now an edit to the renderer alone.
Persistence becomes a port. A one-method interface can be a method reference, here `rows::add`, in tests.
The service only coordinates. It has two collaborators and no rules of its own, so it rarely needs to change.

blocks.text: Payroll code shared by finance, HR and the DBAs.

An `Employee` class held `calculatePay()` for finance, `reportHours()` for HR and `save()` for the database team. HR asked for overtime to be counted differently in reports; both methods shared a helper, so the change silently altered paychecks. Splitting it into `PayCalculator`, `HoursReporter` and `EmployeeRepository` gave each actor a class it can change without touching the others.
Payoff: an HR change can no longer alter a paycheck, and each class has a test suite owned by one team.

lists.title: Use when
items: Two teams or rules regularly edit the same class.
A class needs unrelated dependencies: mailer, tax table and database.
Tests need heavy setup for logic that has nothing to do with it.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The class is small and every method changes together: splitting only adds indirection.
The second reason to change is speculative; split when it appears.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Splitting by technical layer instead of actor yields anemic classes and shotgun surgery.
Pieces with no orchestrator hide the use case across many files.
Separating data from behavior that always change together.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Every small feature touches five files.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records and lambdas make small collaborators cheap, so splitting costs less than it did.
Sealed hierarchies keep variants together when they change together.

rows.difference: SRP isolates one axis of change in one place; OCP then makes that axis extensible without edits.
ISP is SRP seen from the client: narrow the interface to the one role a caller needs.
A facade deliberately aggregates a subsystem for callers. It is fine while it only delegates and holds no rules.
Cross-cutting concerns such as logging or caching can leave a class by wrapping it.
Once responsibilities are split, injection wires the pieces without the pieces knowing each other.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this class most clearly violate?
lines: String name; int hours; long rate;
long calculatePay() { return hours * rate; }              // finance
String hoursReport() { return name + ": " + hours; }      // HR
void save(List<String> db) { db.add(name + "," + rate); } // DBAs

options.why: Finance, HR and the DBAs each have a reason to change this one class.
There is no interface that forces clients to depend on methods they do not use.
There is no subtype relationship, so nothing can fail to substitute.
Nothing here depends on a concrete collaborator; the issue is mixed reasons to change.

exercises.scenario: A `ReportService` was edited four times last quarter: a tax-rate change, a new CSV column layout, an S3 bucket move and a new email subject. Different people made each edit, and two collided in review.
exercises.prompt: What is the most useful refactoring?

options.why: The four edits come from four different reasons. Separate calculation, formatting, storage and delivery so each change lands in one class.
Extension points would help future variants, but they do not separate these four unrelated reasons to change.
The class implements no fat interface; splitting interfaces does not reduce the edits.
Inverting dependencies helps testing, but the class would still hold all four reasons to change.

exercises.prompt: Explain the Single Responsibility Principle in your own words. What counts as a 'responsibility', and what does it not mean?

modelAnswer.text: A responsibility is a reason to change, tied to one actor whose requirements drive that code. A class should answer to one. It does not mean one method or one verb: a cohesive class with many methods is fine. The test is whether unrelated stakeholders can force edits to the same file.

keyPoints: Responsibility = reason to change = one actor
Not 'does one thing' or one method
Smell: unrelated teams editing the same class
Split by axis of change, then compose
